entities.name: Church of Norway
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of Norway (Den norske kirke), established as the state church of Norway from 1537 (following the Lutheran Reformation) until 2017 — when a constitutional amendment finally separated church and state after 480 years of established religion — is now an independent Evangelical Lutheran denomination with approximately 3.5 million members (65% of Norway's population) and is the largest religious organization in Norway. The Church of Norway's transformation from compulsory state church to independent denomination represents the most recent major European church-state separation.

Olaf II (Saint Olaf) Christianized Norway (1014-1028 CE) and the Church of Norway dates its origins to the medieval Catholic church in Scandinavia. The Reformation reached Norway in 1537 under Danish King Christian III — the Norwegian king was simultaneously the Danish king — who established Lutheran Christianity as the state religion, dissolved monasteries, and transferred church property to the crown. This created the 'Evangelical-Lutheran church of the state' that persisted for 480 years.

The 2017 constitutional amendment removed the clause designating the Church of Norway as the state church and established full religious equality — the church became formally independent, employing its own ministers (previously civil servants). The church nonetheless remains culturally dominant: 65% of Norwegians are members (primarily through infant baptism), though regular attendance is among the world's lowest (3-4% weekly). The Church of Norway's open stance on same-sex marriage (approved 2016) made it the world's first national Lutheran church to bless same-sex unions.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of Norway's 2017 separation from the state — ending 480 years of established religion — is the most recent major European church-state separation, and its 2016 same-sex marriage blessing made it the world's first national Lutheran denomination to do so, demonstrating how Scandinavian Lutheranism continues to pioneer social-theological evolution.
